title: Injective homomorphisms of finite-type group schemes are closed immersions
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $A,B$ be separated finite-type $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $u:A\to B$ be a $k$-group-scheme homomorphism. Suppose that $u(R):A(R)\to B(R)$ is injective for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, where $A(R)=\operatorname{Mor}_k(\operatorname{Spec}R,A)$ and similarly for $B$. Then $u$ is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion].

source.place: Proposition 5.31(a) and Theorem 5.34, printed pp.106--107; use the first proof of Theorem 5.34, through the homogeneous-space quotient of Theorem 5.28, not the alternative sketch.

proof.text: The injectivity assumption also holds on points over every $k$-scheme $T$: restrict two maps $T\to A$ to an affine open cover, apply the assumption on each open, and use equality of morphisms locally on their source. Consequently the kernel has exactly the identity point on every test scheme. By the universal property of the kernel fibre product, its projection to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ and its identity section are inverse: test the other composite on the kernel itself, whose inclusion in $A$ must equal the identity-valued map. Thus the scheme-theoretic kernel is trivial.

source.place: Proposition 5.31(a),(b) and the first proof of Theorem 5.34, printed pp.106–107.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-trivial-kernel-homogeneous-quotient] to $H=A$, $G=B$ and $i=u$, using step 1. Obtain $X$, its $B$-action, the point $o$ and the orbit morphism $q:B\to X$. The coset equality with $a=e_B$ gives, for every $k$-scheme $T$,
$$q_T(b)=o_T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\in u_T(A(T)).$$
In particular $q\circ u=o\circ\pi_A$. The quotient theorem assumes trivial kernel, not that $u$ is a closed immersion.

source.place: Proposition 5.31(a),(b) and the first proof of Theorem 5.34, printed pp.106–107.

proof.text: The square with arrows $u:A\to B$, $\pi_A:A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, $q:B\to X$ and $o:\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ is cartesian. Indeed a compatible pair of test maps amounts to $b:T\to B$ satisfying $q_T(b)=o_T$. Step 2 supplies $a:T\to A$ with $u_T(a)=b$, and step 1 makes $a$ unique. This is exactly the universal property of the fibre product, including uniqueness; hence $A$ is that fibre product with projection $u$.

source.place: Proposition 5.31(a),(b) and the first proof of Theorem 5.34, printed pp.106–107.

proof.text: The point morphism $o:\operatorname{Spec}k\to X$ is a closed immersion directly by the affine criterion. For each affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq X$, its inverse image is either empty or all of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, since the latter has one point. In the nonempty case the induced $k$-algebra map $C\to k$ is surjective (it is the identity on constants), so the restriction is $\operatorname{Spec}(C/\ker(C\to k))\to\operatorname{Spec}C$; in the empty case use $C/C=0$. The affine criterion therefore applies on every affine open. Base-change this closed immersion along $q$ using [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change]. By step 3 the resulting projection is $u$, proving the assertion.

source.place: Tag 01QO (lemma-closed-immersion), affine criterion; Tag 01QR (lemma-base-change-closed-immersion), using schemes.tex Tag 01JY (lemma-base-change-immersion).

Step 1: injectivity on points over affine opens extends to every k-scheme T by gluing; the kernel's T-points are then only e, so the kernel is Spec k by the fibre-product universal property. def-sc-group-scheme defines the kernel as A x_{B,u,e} Spec k. The test map b is automatically a k-map; existence comes from step 2 and uniqueness from step 1. Step 4: by the affine criterion stated in def-weil-closed-immersion, each affine preimage o^{-1}(Spec C) is either empty (Spec(C/C)) or Spec k, and a k-algebra map C→k is surjective, so a rational point is a closed immersion with no separatedness of X needed. Small cases checked: trivial H; i an isomorphism; mu_p in G_m in characteristic p with nonreduced T; Borel in GL2 with quotient P^1; Frobenius on G_a, which is excluded because its kernel α_p is nontrivial.
